abstract.para: Snapshots capture the state of a subvolume at a point in time. You can use them to recover earlier versions of files or to return a system to a previous state.

section.title: What is a snapshot?
section.para: A snapshot in Btrfs is a subvolume that shares data with another subvolume. A new snapshot carries the initial content of the original subvolume. Snapshots use the copy-on-write capabilities of Btrfs, so the system creates them quickly with minimal disk space usage.
A snapshot is not a different kind of object. Btrfs treats it like any other subvolume. You can mount it, browse it and delete it with the same tools as other subvolumes.

section.title: Writable and read-only snapshots
section.para: By default, a Btrfs snapshot is writable. Changes to a writable snapshot do not affect the original subvolume. To protect a snapshot against modification, create it as read-only.

Use read-only snapshots for recovery points and for backups. Btrfs requires read-only snapshots as the source for btrfs send. You can create a writable snapshot from a read-only snapshot if you need to modify its content.

section.title: What does a snapshot contain?
section.para: You can only create snapshots of subvolumes. You cannot create a snapshot of an arbitrary directory. A snapshot contains the files of the source subvolume but not the content of nested subvolumes, as described in .
A snapshot always resides on the same Btrfs file system as its source. You cannot store a snapshot on a different file system.
You cannot create a snapshot of a subvolume that contains an active swap file. Deactivate the swap file first.

section.title: Data consistency of snapshots
section.para: Btrfs does not ensure the consistency of application data when it creates a snapshot. If an application writes a file, such as a database, while the snapshot is created, the snapshot can contain a corrupted or partly written file.

important.title: Restoring files from a snapshot can cause problems
important.para: A file that was written during snapshot creation can be corrupted. Restoring such a file causes problems for the application that uses it.
Stop the application or use its own backup function before you create a snapshot. Review the files before you restore them.

section.title: Snapshots and backups
section.para: A snapshot is not a backup. The snapshot and its source share the same blocks on the same device. If the device fails or the file system becomes corrupt, you lose both.
To create a backup, copy the data to a different device or system. For Btrfs, the commands btrfs send and btrfs receive transfer a read-only snapshot to another Btrfs file system. For details, see .
